Wingspan Bird Tier List

Wingspan Bird Tier List

This is a tier list of nearly every bird in Wingspan's digital edition, including all the expansions and promo packs, ranked by a computer player. We built a computer player for Wingspan and had it play 150,000 three-player games against copies of itself. Then we looked at every bird a player drew blind off the deck and asked one question: did the players who got that bird end up further ahead than the players who got some other bird? The answer, in points, is the number under each card. Each tab is a separate list. Pick one, then tap a card for details.

The number is the bird's effect on your final margin (your score minus your best opponent's), compared with an average bird in its place. Nobody chooses the top card of the deck, so across thousands of games everything else washes out and the difference belongs to the bird.

Values by stage. Each bird has five values: one for the starting hand (kept on a coin flip here, so luck again) and one per round. White Stork is +7.9 in the starting hand, +3.5 in round 2 and +1.2 in round 4. The card's number blends the five, leaning on the early rounds because more birds are gained then. Tap a card for all five.

Based on 150,000 games, all played by the computer against copies of itself.

Surprises

  • The base game's famous "Power 4", Common Raven, Chihuahuan Raven, Franklin's Gull and Killdeer, all come out below average on the Oceania mats.
  • Point bombs rule. Nearly every bird worth 8 or 9 points is above average, and they stay strong right through round 4.
  • The promo packs are the strongest birds in the game, ahead of the base game and every expansion.
  • Spangled Drongo is the best bird in the game to find in a starting hand, and nearly worthless by round 2.

The number is the bonus card's effect on your final margin, compared with an average bonus card, measured in the same games and the same way as the birds. Bonus cards arrive blind too, dealt at the start or drawn by a bird's power, so the players who got a given card can be fairly compared with the players who got another. It counts the chance to keep the card, so a card the computer usually throws back scores near zero at best.

Fine print

  • Small differences don't mean much. Each value is good to about ±0.1 points, so cards a few tenths apart are effectively tied.
  • Kept when dealt is the share of the times the card was offered and the computer chose to keep it. Points when kept is the card's average score at game end.
  • A strong computer player's values. These come from the same 150,000 three-player games as the bird list, on the Oceania mats with nectar. Nobody can promise the computer plays perfectly, but it plays well.

The computer player and the community tier lists

  • Wood Duck is as good as people say. Wingsplain's tier list puts Wood Duck in its top "God Tier", and Board Game Arena forum posters call it the strongest card outside the banned list and dead weight if drawn late. The computer agrees on all of it: Wood Duck is one of the best base-game birds, superb in a starting hand and useless in round 4. It also agrees with Wingsplain about Galah, Grey Butcherbird and Sacred Kingfisher.
  • The "Power 4" are overrated. Common Raven, Chihuahuan Raven, Franklin's Gull and Killdeer top the King Panda Games base-game list and an R-bloggers card analysis, and Steam forum players call the Raven overpowered. On the Oceania mats, the computer rates all four below average and almost never plays them. Nobody can promise the computer plays perfectly, and it learned only from games against copies of itself. But it is a strong player, and here the human consensus looks simply wrong for the Oceania game. All four turn your own eggs into food or cards, and that trade seems to have lost its value. Wingsplain's own notes call the Oceania game "egg-starved".
  • Many fan favorites are overrated. Maned Duck, Noisy Miner, Common Chiffchaff and Rainbow Lorikeet sit high on Wingsplain's list and near the bottom of this one. Base-game favorites from forum threads and top-10 articles, such as Spotted Towhee, Gray Catbird, Anna's Hummingbird and Green Heron, also land below average, and the computer hardly ever plays them. These reputations come from the base game, and on the Oceania mats the birds look weaker than their fame.

Patterns across the whole deck

  • Point bombs are great. Printed points matter more than anything else on the card, and nearly every bird worth 8 or 9 points is above average. Food cost is no drawback: at the same points and power, an extra food in the cost makes no measurable difference.
  • Small egg limits are better. Birds holding 0 or 1 egg do clearly better than birds holding 4 or more, even at the same point value. The bonus cards for big egg piles, Oologist and Breeding Manager, are among the worst bonus cards too.
  • Bonus-card birds are strong. Birds that draw bonus cards are mostly above average and grow stronger as the game goes on. Fittingly, Endangered Species Protector, the bonus card for exactly these birds, is the best bonus card by a wide margin.
  • Nectar birds are weak. Nearly every bird with nectar in its cost is below average, and the computer almost never plays them. Spangled Drongo is the exception: it is the single best card to find in a starting hand.
  • Promo birds are the strongest. The promo packs beat the base game and every expansion, even at the same point value. The base game and the three expansions are about equal to one another. The New Zealand and Asia packs are the best, and the UK pack is the only weak one.
  • Card-flipping hunters are strong. Hunters that flip a card from the deck are well above average, and hunters that roll dice are merely average. Every eagle in the game is above average.

Near-twin cards

  • Extra habitats add value. On birds with the same power, each extra habitat is worth about a third of a point, and some cases are far bigger. Chipping Sparrow (forest or grassland) beats Grasshopper, Baird's and Cassin's Sparrows (grassland only) by more than a point with identical cost and power. Three-habitat House Finch likewise beats wetland-only Tree Swallow.
  • On the same power, more printed points help. Many base-game birds share "draw 2 bonus cards, keep 1", and the more points printed on the card, the better the bird, from the 3-pointers up to 8-point Atlantic Puffin. Each extra printed point adds about a third of a point of value. White Stork, the best bird in the game, shares its tray-refresh power with two weaker birds, and its 8 points make the difference.
  • Tuckers need a draw. Brown birds that tuck a card from your hand and draw a replacement are solidly above average. The ones with no draw are below average, and the worst of them, Eurasian Coot, Maned Duck and Rosy Starling, are among the weakest cards in the game. Ruff, which draws a card for every card it tucks, is excellent.

Peak rounds

  • Pink birds peak in the starting hand. Pink birds are the strongest color at three players, but all of their value comes early. They are superb starting-hand cards and slightly below average by round 4. White birds climb from below average in the starting hand to solidly positive later. Yellow birds are the worst color to open with.
  • Some birds are only good early. Spangled Drongo, Wood Duck, Laughing Gull and California Scrub-Jay are among the best starting-hand cards in the game and worth nothing in round 4. The late bloomers are big when-played birds such as Giant Fish Owl, Steppe Eagle and Sulu Hornbill.

Power families

  • Extra-bird powers are weak. Not one bird whose power lets you play another bird at its normal cost is above average. Players prize the saved action, and the computer may underrate it, but at three players it rarely finds these birds worth playing. Yellow-eyed Penguin is the lone exception, one of the best cards in the game, and the difference is the word "free".
  • Sharing powers hurt. Brown powers that give every player the same thing, such as "all players draw a card", cost a big bird about half a point, and they are the main reason some 7-point birds are bad. Giving to one chosen opponent hurts less than giving to everyone. At two players the cost should shrink.
  • Free dice are gold. Powers that give you any die you like from the birdfeeder are all well above average, Eurasian Wren and Laughing Gull especially. Powers that give one named food are below average, and none of the base-game jays and woodpeckers that take "1 seed from the birdfeeder, if available" makes it above average.
  • Spending food for points loses. Brown powers that spend food to tuck cards, lay eggs or draw cards are a losing trade, even among the ones the computer does play. Free caching works: every base-game chickadee and nuthatch that caches a seed from the supply is above average despite its small points.
  • Draw-and-keep powers pay. Powers that draw several cards and let you keep one are worth real points, led by Mandarin Duck and Australian Ibis. Powers that simply draw a card into your hand are all below average.
  • Round-end egg powers are weak. Teal and yellow birds that lay eggs are the weakest birds of their colors. The "lay 1 egg on each of your birds" family is weak at every color, with Say's Phoebe the clear best of them.
  • Some powers go unplayed. Several whole families sit near the bottom because the computer almost never plays them: birds that move themselves to another habitat, birds that copy another bird's power, the European raptors played on top of another bird, and the teal birds that count double toward the round goal. These values mostly reflect the computer's refusal, and a player with a good copy target in view may do better with them.

Bird families

  • Cuckoos are excellent. The cuckoos and cowbirds that lay on another bird when a rival takes the lay-eggs action are nearly all above average, led by Asian Koel, Violet Cuckoo and Common Cuckoo. They are among the birds the computer plays most, and like other pink birds they are best early.
  • Flightless birds are excellent. The kiwis and penguins are among the best cards in the game, and Weka, Takahē and Kākāpō are well above average too. Only Emu and Southern Cassowary fall short.
  • Geese, herons and starlings disappoint. Geese and swans carry plenty of printed points and still come out below average. Herons and egrets are weak too, apart from Black-crowned Night-Heron. Starlings and mynas are all below average, though the computer does play them. Ducks are all over the place, from Wood Duck and Mandarin Duck near the top to Maned Duck near the bottom.

Nests, wingspans and food costs

  • Star nests are best. Birds whose nest counts as any type do clearly better than birds with a fixed nest, even at the same points and egg limit. Round goals and bonus cards keyed to nest types reward a nest that counts as all of them, though these birds may also simply have better powers.
  • Wingspan doesn't matter. At the same point value, big and small birds come out the same, and the bonus cards keyed to wingspan are poor. Big wingspans simply come with big points.
  • Food type barely matters. Birds paid in rodents or fish do a little better than birds paid in invertebrates, and birds paid entirely in seed do a little worse, mostly because the computer rarely plays them. Wild food in the cost makes no difference, and the flexible "or" cost is no bargain.

Expansions, colors and habitats

  • A printed point is worth more in the expansions. Each extra printed point on a bird adds the least value in the base game and the most in the European expansion. The base game's big birds suffer most, for two reasons: its birds with no power at all, such as Wild Turkey and Trumpeter Swan, trail powered birds of the same points by about a point, and its many brown "all players" birds are weak at every point value.
  • European round-end birds are weak. The European expansion introduced the teal round-end power, and its own teal birds are the weakest version of it. Ruff is the big exception. The Asian and promo teal birds do much better, led by Sri Lanka Blue-Magpie, Tufted Puffin and Great Spotted Kiwi.
  • Brown grassland birds are the weakest. Brown birds that live only in grassland are the weakest habitat-and-color group in the game, and most of them are never played. Brown forest and wetland birds do far better, and white grassland birds are fine. The only brown grassland birds that pay are hunters such as Greater Roadrunner. The rest mostly lay or trade eggs, and egg powers lose value on the Oceania mats.

Timing and the tray

  • The starting hand matters most. Birds differ about four times as much in value in the starting hand as in round 4. Maned Duck, the worst opener, costs about 4 points in a starting hand, and no bird drawn in round 4 costs even 1. So the opening keep is the decision to sweat over.
  • Printed points barely matter in the opening hand. Big and small birds are nearly even as starting-hand cards, and from round 2 on the number in the corner becomes the best single guide to a bird's value. Early, the power decides: pink birds, brown card-drawers, flocking birds and hunters make the best opening keeps.
  • Brown card-drawers fade. Brown birds that draw cards are excellent in the starting hand and slightly below average by round 4, and hunters slope the same way. Birds with "all players" powers are a real liability in the starting hand, since the gift to opponents adds up over a whole game, and harmless by round 4.
  • Round-1 filler is weak. The computer plays about a third of its birds in round 1, and the cheap brown birds it plays almost only then are mostly below average. Human players prize a cheap round-1 engine, and some of these cards may do more in human hands, but here they look like plays made for lack of anything better.
  • The tray is a bargain bin. Birds nobody wants sit face up until someone takes them, so the tray is full of weak cards. The computer picks accordingly: it almost always takes a top-tier bird and almost never a bottom-tier one, and when it was forced to take a bottom-tier bird, it lost most of a point.

Bonus cards

  • A bonus card is only as good as its birds. Bonus cards for strong groups of birds are strong, as with Diet Specialist (three-food birds), Rodentologist and Falconer. Bonus cards for weak groups are weak, as with Backyard Birder (cheap birds) and Bird Feeder (seed-eaters). Cartographer is the exception: its birds are ordinary, but a few geography names on the table already pay off.
  • Board-shape bonus cards grow late. Bonus cards for a kind of bird lose value as the game goes on, since there is less time left to collect. Cards that score the shape of your board gain value, since they pay for a board you already have. Mechanical Engineer is the standout.
  • Bonus cards need 3 points. A bonus card that won't reach about 3 points is a net loss. The worst ones pay for leftovers or for runs: Visionary Leader (cards left in hand) is the worst in the box, with Winter Feeder and the Ranger and Data Analyst cards close behind. Endangered Species Protector, Ethologist, Diet Specialist and Cartographer are the best.

Fine print

  • Small differences don't mean much. Each value is good to about ±0.2 points, so birds a few tenths apart are effectively tied.
  • Tray picks are left out. The numbers come only from birds that arrive face down: drawn from the deck, by the draw-cards action or by a bird's power, or dealt into the starting hand. A bird taken from the tray is a choice, so the players who take it aren't a fair comparison.
  • A sharper reading. Each finish is measured against the computer's own guess of it, made just before the card came off the deck. The guess comes before the card, so it can't favor any bird, and it stops a runaway leader from flattering the card they happened to draw.
  • A strong computer player's values. The computer learned the game on its own, with no strategy advice from people, and it only ever played copies of itself. Nobody can promise it plays perfectly, but it plays well, and its disagreements with popular opinion (more on those above) deserve a hearing. In these games it also kept its starting birds on a coin flip and made one tray pick in five at random, for a separate purpose, so it played a little below its usual level.
  • Three-player games on the Oceania mats with nectar. Birds whose worth depends on the number of opponents, pink powers for example, could rank differently at two or four players.
  • Seven birds are missing because the computer can't play their powers yet: the four birds played sideways, Rock Ptarmigan, Ivory Gull and Black-and-White Warbler.
  • Tap any card for a larger view, its value and margin of error, its value at each stage, and the rounds the computer tends to play it in.
